BCG’s analysis of 3,669 public companies finds that generative AI is already reshaping growth strategy—not by replacing its core discipline, but by changing where advantage lies. Leaders must assess both AI’s demand potential and its threat to their existing business model.

AI adoption is becoming a marker of growth leadershipCompanies linking AI to growth initiatives more than doubled from 4.9% before generative AI to 12.7% afterward, with sustained outperformers using it more actively than lagging peers.

Two questions determine the appropriate strategic responseLeaders must judge whether AI creates new demand they can serve and whether it threatens their advantage. Knowledge-based businesses face greater disruption than firms protected by brands or scarce assets.

Companies facing both opportunity and disruption must reinvent firstSoftware and other knowledge-intensive businesses should redesign offerings as AI-first before entrants do. Blockbuster’s failure to respond to online rentals shows why established customer loyalty cannot offset delayed reinvention.

Even less-exposed companies should use AI to improve how they competeConsumer businesses can apply AI across innovation, marketing, and delivery rather than merely adding tools. Domino’s made digital channels central to its operating model; they now generate more than 85% of US sales.

When it comes to growth, AI has two faces: accelerator and potential disrupter. For companies with offerings critical to data center build-outs, it represents a remarkable top-line tailwind. By contrast, it can pose an existential threat to companies with knowledge-based advantages.Leaders are already embracing AI in their growth plans. Some are chasing new and emerging pools of AI-driven demand. Others are using it to turbocharge their innovation and go-to-market approaches and speed up order-to-delivery times. Still others are launching new AI-supported offers and business models. These efforts raise an important question: How quickly should companies act? The lessons from past technological disruptions suggest that time is of the essence: when the game is changing, it’s a good idea to start playing by the new rules.Given that urgency—and because revenue growth accounts for the lion’s share of value creation over the long term—growth is the top issue keeping CEOs awake at night. So, it’s important to understand AI’s impact on your growth strategy.AI doesn’t change the discipline of growth strategy. Rather, it shifts the landscape of advantage and opportunity across which strategies succeed or fail. Our research, analyzing more than 3,600 public companies, suggests that there are four distinct growth strategy approaches. Which one makes the most sense for a company depends on AI’s potential impact on its business.Businesses Are Already Embracing AI for Growth
While organizations had long used earlier forms of AI, such as expert systems or machine learning, the arrival of generative AI in late 2022 was a game changer. And even though the latest AI wave is just gaining strength, our analysis finds a significant increase in the use of AI to sustain, accelerate, and reignite growth.We focused on 3,669 public companies worldwide that reported at least $1 billion in revenue in 2025 and also achieved a growth rate in excess of their industry averages in either or both of two periods: 2017–2022 (before GenAI went mainstream) and 2023–2025 (after GenAI went mainstream).We then analyzed their corporate announcements and shareholder communications and found that the share of companies mentioning AI in connection with growth initiatives more than doubled from 4.9% before GenAI to 12.7% after. Furthermore, companies that sustained, accelerated, or reignited above-average growth from one period to the next leveraged AI significantly more in the GenAI era than those that delivered below-average growth. (See Exhibit 1.)

Even among outperformers, the level of AI adoption varied significantly by industry. Unsurprisingly, tech and related industries led the pack, with 90% of semiconductor companies and 75% of software companies discussing AI in relation to growth. But we also saw notable increases between the two periods elsewhere. For example, 15% of capital goods companies reported AI use in the AI era, up from 2% in the earlier period—as did 11% of utilities, up from 1%.

Strategic Context Matters
All leaders need to consider their AI strategic context when making growth plans, and those contexts can differ a lot. For example, tech companies at the heart of the growth of AI have different opportunities and face different risks than companies focused on branded beverages.In our view, a company’s AI-related strategic context is determined by two factors: which aspects of its business are vulnerable to AI disruption, and what opportunity AI creates for growing the business.Disruption. Does AI pose a threat to the organization’s business model? Or is its impact focused more narrowly on specific internal functions (for example, marketing, finance, manufacturing)?The degree of AI disruption risk is largely associated with an organization’s source(s) of competitive advantage. In general, business models that rely on capability-based competitive advantages (for example, talent, customer insight) are more likely to be disrupted by AI than those with position-based advantages (for example, brand, resource access). (See Exhibit 2.)Opportunity. Is the organization positioned to benefit from growing AI demand by selling products and services that support AI adoption, directly or indirectly? Or is AI attractive primarily as a growth accelerator—making innovation, go-to-market activities, and order-to-delivery processes faster and more effective?Semiconductors, software, and computing hardware clearly benefit from the growth of AI. But other sectors—for example, REITs that control potential data center locations, utilities that provide energy, and telcos that provide connectivity—also benefit from tailwinds of the AI build-out.If past disruptive technologies are a guide, the new types of demand driven by the rise of AI will evolve over time as the technology becomes more mainstream. In the electrification/mass manufacturing revolution of the early 20th century, the initial beneficiaries were machine tool makers like Brown & Sharpe. Then companies brought mass production to more complex goods, as Ford did with autos and Heywood-Wakefield did with furniture. Eventually, companies like Sears, with its catalog, tapped into the new consumer market enabled by the arrival of affordable mass-produced goods.Similarly, with the advent of the internet, benefits initially flowed to infrastructure companies supporting the build-out—fiber, servers, routers, and the like. That infrastructure, in turn, supported the rise of e-commerce, and ultimately search, streaming, social networks, and cloud-based services, including software as a service.

Combining these two dimensions suggests four strategic context archetypes and related growth strategy approaches. (See Exhibit 3.)

Four Growth Strategy Approaches for the AI Era
Growth strategies involve making smart decisions about where to play and how to win. Where to play is about identifying the most attractive markets in which you have a right to win. How to win is about designing the most compelling offer and system to capture a disproportionate share of demand. The four growth approaches we outline here for the AI era are no different.Positioned to benefit from the AI build-out? Catch the wave. This strategy focuses on putting yourself in the path of opportunity. It’s most relevant, at least initially, for companies that can serve demand created by the growth of AI, such as construction, data center equipment, semiconductors, energy solutions, and the like. But over time, it is expected to drive follow-on demand in areas like AI integration services, security, robotics, and more.Here, the strategy is to raise your growth ambition to capture the new AI-related demand while hedging to ensure you retain the loyalty of your most attractive non-AI customers. Given that management attention is finite, it’s critical to ruthlessly prioritize demand pools based on size, profitability, and your right to win—and to keep the focus on both short- and medium-term performance. Move early to lock in key customers and critical partners that enhance your value propositions as you leverage AI to reimagine any functions, such as go-to-market and order-to-delivery, that slow demand capture.Importantly, don’t put all your eggs in one basket. During the dot-com era, many fiber optic players did just that. When the bubble burst, they realized they’d lost touch with many of their traditional customers and applications.Could an AI-first upstart eat your lunch? Reinvent the core. The focus here is on self-disruption. AI can fundamentally reshape your offerings, so it’s existentially important to reimagine the value propositions and capabilities of your products and services with AI before rivals do. This is likely to be the winning strategy for companies in industries whose capability- or knowledge-based advantages are vulnerable to AI, such as CRM, ERP, and other types of software.Here, the strategy is to reimagine your product or service as AI-first. Be clear-eyed about the talent, compute, and data needed to win. Then accelerate growth by building, funding, and executing the operating and capital plans needed to navigate and ensure a seamless transition for customers.A critical pitfall is denial. During the rise of e-commerce, for every Walmart that saw the future and methodically embraced building an online business, there were many that fell by the wayside. Blockbuster Video is the canonical example. It had a strong brand and loyal customers, but it failed to make a decisive move into online rentals and rapidly lost to Netflix.Does AI threaten to erase your advantage? Pivot beyond the core. Where AI has the potential to commoditize your offerings, a growth strategy should focus on radical reinvention. Many business process outsourcing companies, for example, could find themselves disrupted by the rise of agentic AI—and need to chart a new course.This growth strategy approach begins with a dispassionate assessment of which of your traditional sources of competitive advantage remain strong and durable. With that assessment in hand, the next step is to look for attractive value pools in adjacent markets or new frontiers where those advantages can be deployed. And then design a new business model to capture and monetize the opportunity with the highest risk-adjusted value creation potential—leaning on M&A, partnerships, and AI to accelerate the transformation.Fujifilm’s response to the rise of digital photography is a great example. It explored where its expertise in chemicals and advanced materials could be applied and moved successfully into new segments, such as health care, cosmetics, and advanced electronics.Does AI pose neither a market opportunity nor a threat? Step up your game. Here the focus is on accelerating growth by using AI to increase the hit rate of your innovation system, the effectiveness of your go-to-market approach, and the speed of your order-to-delivery processes. This is likely the best strategy in sectors—for example, consumer staples and consumer durables—that benefit by seeing and seizing new trends faster.The imperative here is to identify, function by function, where AI can boost revenue with faster insights, enhanced value propositions, and accelerated execution. Prioritize these functional reinventions by ROI—and as you bring the most promising to life, build a peer-beating capability to experiment with and scale AI. Finally, reinvest some of the gains to strengthen your advantage.Avoid simply “checking the box” without changing the underlying business. The advent of the smartphone didn’t change how you make pizza, but mobile became a new way to connect with pizza lovers. Domino’s understood this and reinvented its entire go-to-market around digital channels—today, mobile and online represent more than 85% of its US sales. Other pizza companies might have introduced an app earlier, but Domino’s won by reorienting its entire business around mobile and other digital channels.

BCG highlights three ways organizations embrace AI: deploy, reshape, and invent. Organizations, of course, deploy it broadly to build fluency across the workforce and enhance everyday tasks like research. However, the real value is created—and competitive advantage strengthened—when AI is used to reshape end-to-end workflows and leveraged to invent new offerings or business models that drive growth.It’s early in the AI era, but companies are already beginning to adapt their growth strategies to their AI strategic contexts. High-performing upper-right quadrant companies, which face both strong AI opportunity and significant disruption risk, are the most engaged with AI for growth. While strong growers in lower-left quadrant sectors, with lower upside opportunity and lower disruption risk, are less likely to embrace AI for growth than those in the upper right, they are ten times more likely to do so than their underperforming peers in the same sectors—quietly changing the game while rivals sleep.So, convene your leadership team and start building a shared understanding of your AI strategic context.What are your critical sources of competitive advantage, and what impact is AI likely to have on them?Are there segments of AI-driven demand you could serve today or that are likely to develop soon?Given the answers to those questions, how should you alter your growth strategy?And finally, what are the implications for your capital plans and timelines?In times of disruption, companies that understand a technology’s strategic implications and act decisively and early are most likely to win the race for growth.
